lithuania.NationalPersonality: Mindaugas's authority rests on his crown, baptism and alliances among ruling families; these do not secure unconditional obedience from local leaders or Samogitians. His court values external recognition while contending with local worship and relatives' claims to land. Limited concessions may buy peace, but promises abroad can weaken cooperation at home.
lithuania.LongTermStrategy:
First preserve communications among the Neman, Neris and the strongpoints of Black Ruthenia, stock grain and livestock, and guard wooded crossings. Seek time through truces, envoys and defined frontier agreements with the Order, while marriage alliances and recognition of particular rights reduce the risk of simultaneous wars with Rus neighbours. Land held by ruling relatives cannot be offered abroad as though it were freely disposable royal property. Negotiate the duration of military service with local leaders: excessive requisitions damage both cultivation and political loyalty. If pressure grows, protect the court, population and routes first, accepting a limited settlement rather than losing domestic followers in a bid for the coast.

The court must distinguish promises abroad from what local leaders have actually accepted. In disputes over succession and estates, use named guarantors and exchanges that can be performed. Religious recognition opens diplomatic channels without replacing consent on the ground. Demands concerning land, service and worship should not be piled together until no group can accept them.

teutonic_order.NationalPersonality: The Order values obedience, its corporate mission and ecclesiastical authorization, yet its Prussian and Livonian branches, bishops and urban merchants have distinct interests. Fortified bases and baptized allies both matter; the prestige of conquest depends on supply, garrison discipline and sustainable rule.
teutonic_order.LongTermStrategy:
Secure shipping, stores and mutual reinforcement among the lower Vistula and Prussian coastal bases before advancing farther inland. Use charters, protected markets and defined rights for converts to attract settlement and cooperation; distinguish negotiation, prisoner exchange and military punishment among hostile communities instead of driving every local group into one coalition. Coordinate seasons and routes with the Livonian branch, negotiating responsibilities with bishops and Danish territory. Expeditions must leave enough men to hold castles and enough grain for winter. If communications fail, shorten supply lines, relieve threatened bases and negotiate a truce rather than treating one victory as permanent possession.

Whether converts and cooperating leaders retain promised standing affects the choices of others. Give officials clear responsibilities and prevent private extortion from provoking resistance. Victory still leaves disputes over captives, land and village supply. Arbitration over episcopal and urban rights can prevent an external campaign from coinciding with conflict within the Order's own sphere.

novgorod.NationalPersonality: Urban autonomy, the faith associated with Saint Sophia and commercial credibility are shared interests, but the assembly, posadnik, archbishop and powerful families compete to define them. Inviting a prince to command does not surrender all civic rights. Wealthy merchants exercise influence without giving every inhabitant an equal voice.
novgorod.LongTermStrategy:
Maintain transport along the Volkhov, Lake Ladoga and the approaches to the Baltic, while protecting the grain channels that feed the city. Sustain foreign trade through defined trading-yard arrangements, adjudication and safe passage; a hasty blockade may injure local markets first. Agree the prince's service, revenues and judicial limits, seek manageable tribute terms with the khan's representatives, and prevent collection disputes from inflaming the urban districts. Ships, hired soldiers and fortifications require funding. If western war coincides with eastern demands, secure food imports, convene negotiations and seek separate settlements, preserving autonomy instead of pursuing a commercial monopoly the city cannot defend.

Urban districts and leading families may disagree over collection, office and military service; an external agreement must identify who pays and who carries it out. Commercial judgments should allow local and visiting traders to anticipate consequences. Keep grain reserves, boat crews and reliable messengers rather than mobilizing the city on one unconfirmed report from a distant war.

kyiv.NationalPersonality: Kyiv retains religious and dynastic prestige, but government after devastation depends on people, functioning towns and outside recognition. Its prince values the Rurikid house and Orthodox institutions while reckoning with local lords and their own followings. An historic title does not automatically deliver tribute from all Rus lands.
kyiv.LongTermStrategy:
Restore settlements, crossings and fields along the Dnieper that can actually be protected, sustaining Kyiv's churches and markets rather than exhausting its inhabitants in contests over titles. Confirm existing rights through envoys to the khan and agreements with neighbours; negotiate passage, marriages and frontier disputes with other Rus princes instead of construing a grant as unrestricted authority to tax them. Maintain the retinue and river transport from revenues that can be collected locally; distant mobilization needs allies and supplies. If steppe armies or neighbours advance, move people and livestock to safety, hold dependable strongpoints and negotiate limited obligations, preserving the manpower needed for recovery.

Churches, townspeople and landholders can provide witnesses, documents and resources for recovery, rather than merely serve as targets for larger exactions. Before accepting claims over former dependencies or relatives, identify actual control and those recognizing it. Prematurely asserting command over all Rus lands burdens limited defences and reconstruction with obligations that cannot be fulfilled.

halych_volhynia.NationalPersonality: The Romanovych house values its royal title, Orthodox traditions and the recovery of towns, while cultivating western courts and the papacy. Princes, boyars and urban communities cooperate and compete. Responses to Mongol pressure must balance honour with the survival of the land rather than reduce policy to revenge.
halych_volhynia.LongTermStrategy:
Secure the roads between Galicia and Volhynia, crossings of the Bug and the fields supplying the towns, assigning defensive responsibilities among the ruling families. Use marriages, recognition of boundaries and specific military assistance in dealings with Poland, Hungary and Lithuania; neighbouring courts are not automatically dependable partners in an anti-Mongol coalition. Fortification and recruitment must match available grain, craftsmen and boyar cooperation, not an unlimited claim based on royal rank. Under coercive demands from the khan's representatives, seek mediation, staged obligations and arrangements that preserve inhabitants. If concessions are unavoidable, protect productive land, succession and networks capable of rebuilding before seeking to restore defences.

Requests for outside help need routes, provisions and an acceptable return; titles or religious undertakings do not guarantee intervention. Leave room for agreement with local houses rather than destroying the service network in an effort to control the boyars. Marriages and estates assigned to royal relatives should sustain cooperation, not treat children as pledges that can be promised repeatedly.

prussia.NationalPersonality: Local clans and leaders cooperate through kinship, custom and worship, responding differently to the Order's demands, landholding and missions. Some resist, others negotiate or accept baptism. Collective defence requires protection and a fair sharing of burdens rather than presumed obedience to one royal authority.
prussia.LongTermStrategy:
Preserve villages, grain stores and wooded escape routes, using known rivers, lakes and tracks to impede enemy concentration without exhausting inhabitants against strong castles. Leaders should specify obligations for reinforcements, supplies and prisoner exchange, seeking concrete assistance from Lithuania and neighbouring groups. Protecting cultivation and displaced families strengthens a coalition more reliably than plunder; severing trade also deprives local people of salt and iron. If a siege cannot be sustained, disperse, conserve seed and livestock, and negotiate over land and customary rights. Continuing cooperation matters more than a single fierce oath.

Clans differ in enemies, harvest schedules and available fighters; joint action needs a meeting place, retreat and limit to a siege. Distinguish the actions of people who trade with the Order or accept baptism instead of alienating every possible intermediary. Protecting dependants, returning identified captives and limiting internal reprisals preserve trust for another mobilization.

baltic_tribes.NationalPersonality: The tribes prize local autonomy, kinship assistance and customs governing land, while their leaders also dispute territory and old grievances. Resistance to outside control can coexist with trade, marriage or limited dependence. Alliances require specific consent; related religious traditions do not replace negotiation.
baltic_tribes.LongTermStrategy:
Defend the settlements and forest routes of each community, arranging warning, mutual assistance and evacuation with neighbouring clans. Negotiate passage, markets and military obligations separately with the Lithuanian court, the Order and Rus neighbours rather than promising troops on behalf of every tribe. Maintain followers through acceptable shares of provisions, protection and captured goods; repeated raids may invite reprisals and destroy trading partners. If concentrated forces cannot be resisted, preserve the population through dispersed strongpoints and seek temporary protection or a limited settlement that leaves local leaders a voice.

Agreements with an outside protector should specify duration, numbers and who represents which community, preventing one private promise from becoming a permanent obligation for all. Escorting traders and retaining access to salt and iron reduce the costs of prolonged conflict. Respected relatives can mediate internal disputes, restoring passage and assistance before a new joint expedition.

estonia.NationalPersonality: Danish royal authority, local vassals, churches and port communities all shape government in northern Estonia, with rights that do not always coincide. Maritime connections and Reval's defences provide security but make rulers dependent on shipping and local cooperation. Collection of dues must reckon with cultivators and merchants.
estonia.LongTermStrategy:
Hold Reval's port, northern roads and shipping links with Denmark, supplying the garrison and defences before considering an eastern advance. Agree frontier patrols, trade and judicial responsibilities with the Livonian branch and bishops; an uncoordinated raid may turn a dispute with Rus neighbours into a wider war. Port and estate revenues must pay for troops, crews and repairs rather than serve as an unlimited reserve. If shipping fails or vassals withhold service, concentrate on defensible port towns, obtain merchant transport and local compromises, and restore supplies through negotiation.

Orders across the sea can arrive late, so local officials need verified reports for immediate defence and reserves while awaiting help. Local converts, vassals and merchants must know the limits of requisition and jurisdiction. When promised protection fails, heavier penalties may drive villagers away and interrupt transport, weakening coastal government further.

polack.NationalPersonality: Trade along the Western Dvina, the local princely house and churches sustain Polotsk's position, while Lithuanian power and Livonian towns influence its choices. The court values local jurisdiction and dues, but historic independence cannot substitute for negotiations with stronger neighbours.
polack.LongTermStrategy:
Secure shipping, crossings and town supplies along the Western Dvina, agreeing passage, compensation and dues with Riga's merchants and riverside lords. Define obligations or cooperation with Lithuania, using marriage and envoys to limit uncertain service demands without provoking a blockade through abrupt changes of allegiance. Support the retinue and defences from sustainable river trade and estates. If the route is severed, restore transport, reduce distant campaigning and seek shared guarantees rather than exhausting local resources in a struggle for every toll station.

Passage and local justice cannot simply be left to a distant ally; seizures and raids require witnesses, compensation and deadlines. Protecting towns, boat crews and riverside settlements preserves dues and resources for independent negotiation. The stronger an outside lord's claim becomes, the more carefully one must distinguish a particular service from a permanent change in local rights.

pomerania.LongTermStrategy:
Maintain links among the duchy's ports, river mouths and agricultural hinterland, clarifying town charters, seigneurial jurisdiction and ducal dues. Use marriages, frontier agreements and outside recognition to gain space in dealings with Brandenburg and the Polish principalities; negotiate transport and market security with sea traders. Pay for war from actual estates and agreed contributions rather than assuming a right to tax the entire Baltic coast. If the frontier gives way, preserve people, core ports and bargaining assets, seeking a conditional truce before several districts rebel at once.

Inviting settlers and granting town charters can increase long-term income while altering relations with nobles; specify land, jurisdiction and service. Shipping depends on merchant vessels and seasons, so commercial standing is not an immediately available fleet. Outside assistance needs limits, arbitration and terms of redemption to prevent a short-term loan or military promise from becoming irreversible territorial loss.

krakow.LongTermStrategy:
Secure Kraków, Sandomierz and the crossings, stores and roads between them, arranging reconnaissance, defence and shelter for inhabitants. Reduce internal Polish war through dynastic negotiation and church mediation, seeking concrete assistance from Galicia and Hungary rather than substituting an alliance title for troops and grain that can arrive. Match repairs, the retinue and levies to available means, avoiding labour demands that prevent harvest. If steppe armies approach, protect people, livestock and seed, concentrate on defensible places and seek relief instead of making every outer settlement a test of honour.

Establish what relatives, churches and towns can actually supply before promising compensation to foreign helpers. Keep channels for reports and envoys during alarm instead of relying on unverified enemy numbers. smolensk.LongTermStrategy:
Protect the upper Dnieper, routes toward the Western Dvina and urban food supplies, maintaining established trade and judicial arrangements with Riga and Gotland merchants. Use envoys, compensation and frontier agreements to reduce seizures and reprisals, seeking arbitration in dynastic disputes before mobilizing. Account separately for trade dues, estates and tribute obligations rather than treating passing merchants' wealth as freely available war finance. If roads or shipping are threatened, restore safe passage, protect commercial credibility and hold core nodes, preserving income and inhabitants through a limited settlement.
